questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium bromide. The solution turns orange. What has happened?

options.text: Chlorine has dissolved to form a coloured solution but no reaction occurred
Chlorine has displaced bromine from potassium bromide because chlorine is more reactive
Bromine has displaced chlorine because bromine is more reactive
The potassium has reacted with chlorine to form a coloured compound

questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine (higher in Group 7), so it displaces bromine from potassium bromide: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. The orange colour is due to the bromine that has been released into solution. More reactive halogens can always displace less reactive ones from their salts.

questions.stem: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, while astatine is the least reactive. What is the best explanation for this trend?

options.text: Fluorine has more electron shells, making it easier to attract electrons
Astatine has fewer protons, so it attracts electrons less strongly
Going down the group, the outer shell is further from the nucleus with more shielding, so it is harder to attract an extra electron
Going down the group, atoms have fewer electrons in their outer shell

questions.explanation: All halogens have 7 outer electrons and need to gain 1 electron to react. Going down the group, atoms get larger with more electron shells providing increased shielding. The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker, making it harder to gain that electron.

questions.stem: At room temperature, fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid. If you could observe astatine, what state would you predict?

options.text: A gas, following the same pattern as the other halogens
A solid, as boiling points increase going down Group 7
A liquid, as it would be similar to bromine
It could be any state since there is no clear trend

questions.explanation: There is a clear trend: melting and boiling points increase going down Group 7 due to stronger intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces) between larger molecules. The progression from gas (F₂, Cl₂) to liquid (Br₂) to solid (I₂) continues, so astatine would be predicted to be a solid at room temperature.

questions.stem: A student adds bromine water to potassium chloride solution and observes no colour change. They conclude bromine must be unreactive. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: The student is correct — bromine is unreactive
Bromine cannot displace chlorine because bromine is less reactive than chlorine
The reaction is too slow to observe
Bromine water is too dilute to react

questions.explanation: A halogen can only displace a less reactive halogen from a compound. Since bromine is below chlorine in Group 7, it is less reactive and cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride. Bromine is certainly reactive — it just cannot displace a more reactive halogen. This is a displacement reaction principle.

questions.stem: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid. When sodium reacts with chlorine gas, it forms sodium chloride. What type of bonding is present in each compound?

options.text: Both have ionic bonding
HCl has covalent bonding; NaCl has ionic bonding
Both have covalent bonding
HCl has ionic bonding; NaCl has covalent bonding

questions.explanation: Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so HCl is formed by covalent bonding (sharing electrons). Sodium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so NaCl is formed by ionic bonding (transfer of electrons from sodium to chlorine). Halogens can form both types of bond depending on what they react with.
